title: Letter to the editor: Is South African wine really too cheap?
summary:
The following received via email from Louis Vigneault-Dubois, a former diplomat and WSET Level 2-certified wine enthusiast: Last week, I read Tim Atkin’s annual South Africa Special Report with great interest, and one argument in particular stayed with me: that South African wines remain too cheap internationally. Having spent the past five years living in […]

The post Letter to the editor: Is South African wine really too cheap? appeared first on winemag.
content:
The following received via email from Louis Vigneault-Dubois, a former diplomat and WSET Level 2-certified wine enthusiast:

Last week, I read Tim Atkin’s annual South Africa Special Report with great interest, and one argument in particular stayed with me: that South African wines remain too cheap internationally.

Having spent the past five years living in South Africa and discovering its extraordinary wine scene, I have a lot of sympathy for that view. But after recently moving back to Germany, I’m seeing the question of value from a different perspective.

Let’s look at white wine in particular. A small moment in a wine shop recently summed it up perfectly.

On a hot August evening, a young woman walked in looking for a fresh white wine to take to an open-air concert with friends. Her budget was around €15 (R280).

The cheapest South African white on the shelf was Ken Forrester Old Vine Reserve Chenin Blanc at €18 (R335). The next on the price scale was Luddite Saboteur White at €24 (R450).

A few shelves away were several excellent German Rieslings, Pinot Gris and more at €15–16 (R280–300), some even carrying the VDP Erste Lage designation, loosely comparable to Premier Cru.

The salesperson made a convincing case for the Ken Forrester Chenin. But the customer chose a German white.

Not because it was necessarily better. It was slightly cheaper, more familiar and felt like the safer choice.

That small interaction captures what I think is one of the challenges facing South African wine in Europe.

The producer’s price isn’t the consumer’s value

I completely agree that many South African growers are not paid enough. Old vines, low yields and quality viticulture are expensive and increasingly difficult to sustain at current prices.

But what producers need to charge and what international consumers perceive as value are two different questions.

Many of the interesting South African wines I encounter in Germany seem to start around €20 and quickly move into the €30–40 range and above. For an enthusiast who understands what an old-vine Chenin from the Swartland or Stellenbosch represents, these wines can offer exceptional value.

For the broader consumer, however, €30 or €40 is already firmly premium territory.

Competition is fierce

In Germany, the €10–20 segment for white wine is packed with excellent Riesling, Grauburgunder and Weissburgunder, alongside Austrian Grüner Veltliner, Italian and Spanish whites, Loire Sauvignon Blanc, Rhône blends and entry-level Chablis.

Consumers are not only faced with an enormous range of familiar alternatives; many European producers also prominently market their organic, biodynamic or sustainability credentials, messages that may resonate more strongly with today’s European consumer than, for example, an old-vine certification.

What I see far less often are compelling South African whites in that price category that can persuade a curious but relatively casual wine drinker to take a chance on the Cape.

South Africa certainly has the story: extraordinary old vines, distinctive terroirs and a generation of exceptional winemakers. Critics know it. Serious wine lovers increasingly know it.

But the average European consumer probably doesn’t know what Stellenbosch, Swartland or Hemel-en-Aarde represent, let alone who Eben Sadie, Chris Alheit or the Mullineux are.

And as prices rise, that lack of recognition matters even more. A €20 South African Chenin is no longer competing simply with other Chenins. It is competing for the same money a consumer might spend on a serious German Riesling, a Chablis, Sancerre or any number of established European wines and regions backed by decades, sometimes centuries, of consumer recognition.

For South African producers and grape growers, the uncomfortable reality is that making excellent wine and having a compelling story is not enough. Plenty of other wine regions can offer both.

Among casual drinkers, price remains a crucial part of the value equation. And this is where South Africa seems to struggle: consumers can often find very good wines from more familiar regions at a cheaper price. However good the South African bottle may be, that makes it a harder choice on the shelf.

Bridging the price gap

The answer for the industry, therefore, cannot simply be to push prices upwards. It also has to be about strengthening the value proposition and building recognition across different price points.

Someone who discovers a brilliant South African Chenin for €10 today is far more likely to spend €30, €50 or €60 on a serious bottle tomorrow. But if the choice is between an €6 supermarket “dry white” and a €30 specialist bottle, we are asking consumers to skip several rungs of the ladder.

South Africa needs those intermediate rungs: wines that are accessible enough to encourage discovery, distinctive enough to create an association with the Cape, widely available enough to build recognition, and compelling enough to make consumers want to take the next step.

Ultimately, the question may not be whether South African wine is really too cheap internationally, but whether it has the right proposition at every level of the market to bring consumers along on the journey, from an accessible first bottle, to the middle ground, and eventually to the country’s great wines.

The quality is already there at the top. The challenge is building the steps that lead consumers there.

The post Old Vine Report 2026: Call for entries appeared first on winemag.
content:
Entries for the third annual Old Vine Report are now open – wines must be made from Certified Heritage Vineyards (vines that are 35 years and older vines registered with SAWIS and approved by the Old Vine Project).

The report will be based on the outcome of a blind tasting of wines entered within a specific category and includes key findings, tasting notes for the Top 10 wines, buyer’s guide and scores on the 100-point quality scale for all wines entered.

Wines will be tasted by a three-person panel consisting of Christian Eedes as chairman, James Pietersen, CEO of of Wine Cellar, Cape Town merchants and cellarers of fine wine, and Francois Rautenbach, a hospitality and wine specialist, scoring done according to the 100-point system.

Prize

The producer of the wine judged Best Overall wins a FERMTECH SOLUTIONS organic fermentation kit worth approximately R10,000.

Enter now

For the rules and entry form, click here.

title: Old Vine Report 2026: Rules and entry form
summary:
Rules Wines must be certified as South African and made from Certified Heritage Vineyards (vines that are 35 years and older vines registered with SAWIS and approved by the Old Vine Project). Wines entered must be current release or soon to be released (minimum stock requirement: 50 x 6 bottles). Producers may enter as many […]

The post Old Vine Report 2026: Rules and entry form appeared first on winemag.
content:
Rules

  • Wines must be certified as South African and made from Certified Heritage Vineyards (vines that are 35 years and older vines registered with SAWIS and approved by the Old Vine Project).
  • Wines entered must be current release or soon to be released (minimum stock requirement: 50 x 6 bottles). Producers may enter as many different wines as they see fit.
  • An entry sample takes the form of two bottles. There are two submission methods – please indicate the number corresponding to your chosen option on the entry form:
  1. collection by Aspiring Couriers (login and create a waybill here)
  2. delivery to Aspiring Couriers
  • Entries close Wednesday 7 October. The deadline for the submission of samples is 17h00 on Thursday 8 October. LATE SUBMISSIONS WILL NOT BE ACCEPTED.
  • In the event a wine achieves Top 10 status, 18 bottles must be set aside at no charge, these to be served at promotional events.

To enter, kindly ensure you (or the company you represent) are a subscriber to Winemag.co.za. If you’re not yet subscribed, click here to sign up.

An entry fee of R1,495 including VAT per wine applies and you will be directed to our online shop to make payment after you have completed the entry form below. Please note that if you want to enter multiple wines, each will require a separate form although payment can be made all at once.

title: Aspiring Top Drop Awards 2026: 22 wines delivering exceptional value
summary:
We tasted 92 wines retailing for R120 or less. Twenty-two scored 91 points or higher, qualifying them to carry the Top Drop sticker. From these, we’ve selected 10 standout buys – wines that combine particularly high quality with an especially attractive price. The remaining 12 also qualify as Top Drops and are listed below. The post Aspiring Top Drop Awards 2026: 22 wines delivering exceptional value appeared first on winemag.
content:
We tasted 92 wines retailing for R120 or less. Twenty-two scored 91 points or higher, qualifying them to carry the Top Drop sticker.

From these, we’ve selected 10 standout buys – wines that combine particularly high quality with an especially attractive price. The remaining 12 also qualify as Top Drops and are listed below.

Top 10 Best Buys

Ranked by quality, with price considered in assessing overall value.

1. Nederburg Baronne 2024

44% Cabernet Sauvignon, 42% Shiraz, the rest Petit Verdot, Tannat, Durif, Malbec and Carignan. Engaging aromatics of red and black berries, fynbos, flowers and a hint of pepper. Light-bodied with fresh acidity and a gently savoury finish. Not massively intense in terms of weight or flavour, but by no means simple – unshowy and highly likeable.

Score:

93

Price:

R100

2. Wild House Chardonnay 2025 (Wildeberg)

Top notes of flowers and herbs before lemon, peach and the merest hint of vanilla on the nose while the palate is rich and textured but equally vital thanks to vibrant acidity. Well balanced and rather seductive.

Score:

93

Price:

R110

3. De Wet Chenin Blanc 2026

Very primary and inviting aromatics of guava, citrus and peach plus hints of flowers and herbs. The palate is clean and fresh with good fruit concentration, crisp acidity and a dry finish. Well balanced and entirely unassuming.

Score:

92

Price:

R69

4. Riebeek Cellars Collection Shiraz 2025

Just a little flinty reduction gives way to red berries, fynbos, rose and white pepper on the nose. The palate is light-bodied with juicy fruit, fresh acidity and fine tannins, with a faint savoury quality to the finish. Modest in scale but full of appeal.

Score:

92

Price: 

R88

5. Leyland Chenin Blanc 2026 (De Wet)

Aromatics of herbs, lime, lemon, a hint of guava and touch of leesy complexity. The palate has good weight and texture, with moderate acidity providing balance and a gently savoury finish bringing it to a neat close.

Score:

92

Price: 

R90

6. Durbanville Hills Cabernet Sauvignon 2024

Red and black berries, some leafiness, with a pleasant hint of smokiness on the nose. The palate is clean and fresh with fine tannins, the finish dry. True to the variety, unimposing, honest.

Score:

92

Price: 

R100

7. Koelenbosch Shiraz 2023 (Koelenhof)

The nose shows red and black berries, a touch of violets and black pepper. The palate is luscious and juicy with moderate acidity and a gently savoury finish.

Score:

92

Price: 

R105

8. Bellingham Homestead Sauvignon Blanc 2025

Herbal notes lead into bell pepper, grapefruit, granadilla and pineapple on the nose. The palate is rich and rounded, with well-integrated, tangy acidity and a gently savoury finish. At this price, it’s difficult to ask for much more.

Score:

92

Price: 

R115

9. Zorgvliet Silver Myn Argentum 2024

56% Merlot, 27% Cabernet Franc, 14% Cabernet Sauvignon, 3% Petit Verdot. Red and black berries, violets, a leafy note, earth and meat stock on the nose. Medium bodied with juicy fruit, good freshness and fine tannins. Lively with a nicely savoury finish. Classic in style, unshowy in execution.

Score:

92

Price: 

R118

10. Salt Rock Chenin Blanc 2025

Attractive aromatics of honeysuckle, herbs, citrus and green apple. The palate has concentrated fruit yet comes across as taut and austere in structure, with punchy acidity and a particularly dry finish. Elegant and nuanced.

Score:

92

Price: 

R120

Also Top Drop

These 12 wines also scored 91 points or higher and retail for R120 or less.

What is a Top Drop?

Top Drop is Winemag’s shortlist of wines that combine high quality with affordability. To qualify, a wine had to retail for R120 or less and score at least 91 points in our tasting.

Look for the Top Drop sticker in stores.

Winner benefits

Each category winner received R5,000 in shipping from Aspiring Couriers.

title: Burgundy dominates the world’s most expensive wines
summary:
Burgundy’s dominance at the top end of the fine-wine market is extraordinary. Investment platform WineCap’s 2026 ranking of the 25 most expensive wines contains 24 Burgundies, with only Domaine Jean-Louis Chave’s Ermitage Cathelin from the northern Rhône breaking the region’s hold. Even more striking, 17 wines come from Domaine Leroy and Domaine d’Auvenay, both owned […]

The post Burgundy dominates the world’s most expensive wines appeared first on winemag.
content:
Burgundy’s dominance at the top end of the fine-wine market is extraordinary. Investment platform WineCap’s 2026 ranking of the 25 most expensive wines contains 24 Burgundies, with only Domaine Jean-Louis Chave’s Ermitage Cathelin from the northern Rhône breaking the region’s hold.

Even more striking, 17 wines come from Domaine Leroy and Domaine d’Auvenay, both owned by Lalou Bize-Leroy, together accounting for 64.1% of the ranking’s combined value.

At the top is Domaine de la Romanée-Conti’s Romanée-Conti Grand Cru at £195,406 per 12-bottle case (roughly equivalent to R352,000 a bottle at today’s exchange rate), followed by Domaine d’Auvenay’s Chevalier-Montrachet Grand Cru at £186,419 per case (R336,000 a bottle).

For perspective, Pétrus, Bordeaux’s highest-ranked wine, sits only 46th in the wider ranking, while Krug Clos du Mesnil, Champagne’s highest entry, is 80th.

The lesson is fairly simple. At the very top of the wine market, scarcity, provenance and reputation can count for more than points. Burgundy happens to possess extraordinary quantities of all three – but the remarkable concentration of value around Lalou Bize-Leroy suggests that, at this level, the market is pricing not just wine but access to something that cannot readily be reproduced.

title: Jamie Goode: Old vines won’t survive on sentiment alone
summary:
Wine has been going through some changes. It has always been going through changes, to be honest. In classic wine-producing regions, we’ve had a long shift from the need for large quantities of cheap wine to feed the heroic thirst of the masses. People in Portugal, France, Italy and Spain used to drink a lot […]

The post Jamie Goode: Old vines won’t survive on sentiment alone appeared first on winemag.
content:
Wine has been going through some changes. It has always been going through changes, to be honest. In classic wine-producing regions, we’ve had a long shift from the need for large quantities of cheap wine to feed the heroic thirst of the masses. People in Portugal, France, Italy and Spain used to drink a lot of wine. The big need was for volume, and so industries geared to supply lots of cheap wine have been retrofitted to produce better quality wine for a more discerning and less thirsty customer base. It has been an uncomfortable process, and it’s still ongoing. In other countries wine has been growing and people have been drinking more, but even this growth has seen a bit of contraction of late. And it’s uncomfortable to watch, because people and their livelihoods are impacted.

The danger is that in this contraction process, it’s not only the less impressive vineyards that are being pulled out, but also some rather special vineyards. A case in point is in the notorious vine pull in Australia in the 1980s, where some very special old vineyards in regions such as the Barossa were taken out. Because of the absence of phylloxera in South Australia, the Barossa has a lot of old, ungrafted vines. There are more than 100 hectares of centenarian vineyards there.

And in Spain, were it not for the efforts of Comando G and their buddies, many of the amazing old Garnacha vineyards that simply weren’t profitable would have been pulled out. It’s strange how fashion changes: in the peak Parker era everyone wanted big, dark, bold wines – something that Garnacha can’t do easily. Now we cherish the fragrant, lighter-coloured reds that old vine Garnacha is an absolute specialist at.

Globally, there are many special old vineyards. They are a treasure, but they aren’t always treasured. Should there be laws protecting them?

When I was at university, one of the courses I took in my degree in biological science was on conservation and wildlife management. I really enjoyed it, to the point that I even considered doing a research job in ecology. There were two things I took away from this course. One is that if you want to conserve rare species, you need to focus on preserving their habitat. The second was that the only conservation that really works is conservation that pays. If an ecosystem or a species becomes an economic resource, then people will preserve them.

This is exactly the approach that has been taken by the Old Vine Project in South Africa, and it has been fantastic to watch this amazing initiative develop. And I guess imitation is the sincerest form of flattery: the model has been adopted by others. When Rosa Kruger set out to produce a list of vineyards over 35 years old in South Africa, this gave producers in search of old vines a chance to connect with growers. Previously, the fruit from many of these vineyards was being sold too cheaply, and disappearing into big blends where its origin was never recognized.

How do you keep precious old vineyards in the ground, rather than let them be bulldozed? I guess you could give them protected status, but for a vineyard to continue, it has to be farmed, and you can’t force a farmer to maintain a vineyard if they aren’t making money for it. And governments can’t easily pay farmers to preserve some vineyards and not others.

The best way to keep great vines in the ground is to value them. And the Old Vine Project does just this. Winemakers with ambition buy grapes from heritage vineyards and pay a premium that makes farming them pay. The growers are rewarded, and the bulldozers stay away. The Old Vine heritage seal is a great initiative here, and it means that suddenly cooperatives who were previously putting old vine grapes into an inexpensive wine can now make a separate wine from the old vines, add the heritage sticker, and charge R200 for the bottle. The seal acts as a strong buying cue. Everyone benefits.

Part of the dynamic here is having ambitious landless winemakers who want to make something special, and are able to because there is a culture of growers owning vineyards who are willing to sell these grapes. South Africa has a nice dynamic where winemakers working for large companies are allowed to do a bit of home brew: to start their own brand. Sometimes there are restrictions: perhaps a case limit of the new brand, or a stipulation that they use varieties other than used by their employer, to avoid conflict of interest situations. But the general permissiveness of winery owners in allowing their winemakers to have side projects is good for everyone, I think. It keeps the winemaker fulfilled professionally, it allows them to build their own brand gradually, and the dynamism created by new producers and new projects is good for the overall health of South African wine.

And, of course, this creates customers for old heritage vineyards, keeping them in the ground.

On a regional level, there is something to be said for legislation to protect significant vineyards. This is important where land has value for redevelopment. If it is zoned so that no one can build homes, but it has to be kept as agricultural land, then this is valuable. Urban spread is threatening many wine regions, and some legislation could help here. I was recently in the Hunter Valley, a brilliant historically significant Australian wine region. With its proximity to Sydney, this is quite a playground for city folk. If economics is left to decide the destiny of the land, then it’s likely that the vineyard area will further contract. You could end up with a wine region popular with tourists, but with hardly any vineyards.

But the best way to preserve important vineyards? Make them pay!

  • Jamie Goode is a London-based wine writer, lecturer, wine judge and book author. With a PhD in plant biology, he worked as a science editor, before starting wineanorak.com, one of the world’s most popular wine websites.

title: Tim James: Capaia – the wine dream that went bust
summary:
There’s a good chance that younger readers of this website will not even have heard (vaguely, perhaps?) of Capaia, a fairly large wine estate in the Philadelphia ward (even heard of that more than vaguely?) not far from Cape Town. But Capaia was gleaming on the horizon hopefully and brightly two decades back, having been […]

The post Tim James: Capaia – the wine dream that went bust appeared first on winemag.
content:
There’s a good chance that younger readers of this website will not even have heard (vaguely, perhaps?) of Capaia, a fairly large wine estate in the Philadelphia ward (even heard of that more than vaguely?) not far from Cape Town. But Capaia was gleaming on the horizon hopefully and brightly two decades back, having been founded in 1997, with an auspicious first bottling of a Bordeaux-style blend in 2003. The 2006 Grape poll to find the Cape’s top producers also asked voters about promising newcomers, and Capaia was the best-performing red wine in that category.

But the days of glory were short-lived. It’s an interesting and significant story, and on Thursday this week Capaia is going on auction (for details see here, if you’re a potentially interested party, or just want more details about the property and some eyebrow-raising claims about its eminence).

Established with panache on the rolling hills of a former wheat-farm on the edge of the Swartland, Capaia was back then a major German investment in the Cape. Although I dare say a lot of money was saved by buying land here rather than an established property in Stellenbosch, no expense was spared in vineyards or winery – for example, one of the world’s largest arrays of wooden fermenters was built onsite by Taransaud.

It was all the creation of Baron Alexander von Essen (pretty significant as an aristocrat, it seems, also a wine merchant back home) and his architect baroness, Ingrid – she came from the immensely rich family that owned the Miele domestic appliances company. So Europe’s feudal nobility and European capital ruled, and there seemed from the start to be not all that much faith in South Africa to provide more than the soil, and labour. The Herr Baron had great contacts back home, of course, and immediately brought in the eminent Hungarian winemaker Tibor Gál, most famous for building the reputation of the super-Tuscan Ornellaia. Czech-born New Zealand winegrown Daniel Schuster came in to oversee the vineyard planting (with imported virus-free material), as presumably the locals couldn’t be trusted. From another great aristocratic family came Italian Ludovico Antinori – advising in some capacity, I guess, or at least lending a suitable, classy glow.

Jan Coetzee was some sort of local advisor, and Tertius Naudé was appointed “winemaker-in-residence”, as Platter’s put it at the time. (I think it was more than rumour that the local winemaking hack was obliged to call his employers Sir and Madam). But the grand foreign contingent was what it was all about.

Tragically, Tibor Gál died in a car accident on Helshoogte in February 2005. He’d made two excellent vintages of Capaia, the flagship red. In 2011 I noted that the Capaia 2004 “fulfilled my hopes of half a decade ago” (tasting it for Platter 2006). The same year I also wrote about the “rather handsome, burly 2003 … still very much alive, with good fruit, well balanced and with some complexity and not too much sweetness, showing the potential of these Philadelphia vineyards.” The wines were big and bold, certainly, in the Parkerist fashion of the time. I later lamented about the 2009 Capaia that it was spoilt by over-ripeness (I was mostly referring to this character of many Michel Rolland-influenced wines here). Too often, I suggested, winemakers from classic regions came to the New World and forgot all about claims of elegance and, usually pretty disastrously, pursued the extreme ripeness that didn’t come naturally in most of Europe.

The death of Tibor Gál led to another European aristocrat – but this one also also a leading Bordelais winemaker, Baron/Comte/Graf/Earl Stephan von Neipperg (I’ve seen all those titles used) – being taken on as consultant. He seems to have been also a friend, and stayed as a permanent presence, eventually taking an ownership share in 2015, after the breakup of the Von Essen marriage and the Baroness’s sole proprietorship. It didn’t, frankly, seem to lead to great things in terms of wine. Nor had the consultancy of a famous Austrian winemaker, Manfred Tement, designed to raise the profile of the white wines.

The most serious consequence of Gál’s death was a period of instability in the winemaking at Capaia, from which the estate seems to never really have recovered. There was a rapid turnover for a while of local winemakers – basically as assistants to the famous European consultants. Were they ever respected? Ever allowed to make decisions as and when they were needed?

A time of stability did emerge with the arrival of Bernabé Strydom as cellarmaster – the first local to have that title recorded in Platter’s. But the reputation of the wines never really recovered. As far as I know, the always-important connections established with the German market became increasingly significant for sales. But a good part of the farm’s annual grape-harvest must have been sold off.

Capaia was perhaps generally unlucky. A local accountant, for example, defrauded them of R17 million before being found out. In 2021 Ingrid von Essen died, and the von Essen couple’s daughter Mariella took ownership, along with the faithful Comte Stephan von Neipperg.

But, at last, they clearly want out. And so to this auction. The starting price is set at just under R50 million. Is that a lot or a little? It doesn’t seem much, but I’m not in a position to know. Something must depend on the state of the 50-odd hecares of vines and a few more of olives (and many more unfarmed). Platter’s 2026 says that the winery was last year “slated for a major revamp” – did this happen or is it still needed? As to the value of the brand, it is surely pretty negligible – the 2022 flagship red Capaia is available (if you look hard, or on the website) for under R200, and Germany seems to constitute the international market. R50 million is not a vast amount in European money, but, also, Philadelphia remains not as desirable an address for investors as Constantia or Stellenbosch.

It’s all rather sad, in fact. So much aristocratic and metropolitan arrogance, its money spent and probably largely wasted on this adventure. It was a time when Cape wine and a new breed of local winemakers and viticulturists were on the threshold of proving themselves internationally – but this movement was apparently untrusted by at least these newcomers. Germans have been great contributors to winemaking here from the beginning (see here and here), but the Capaia intervention just didn’t work out, and looks like it’s coming to an end – soon, if this auction works.

  • Tim James is one of South Africa’s leading wine commentators, contributing to various local and international wine publications. His book Wines of the New South Africa – Tradition and Revolution appeared in 2013.

title: Letter to the editor: Is South African wine really too cheap?
summary:
The following received via email from Louis Vigneault-Dubois, a former diplomat and WSET Level 2-certified wine enthusiast: Last week, I read Tim Atkin’s annual South Africa Special Report with great interest, and one argument in particular stayed with me: that South African wines remain too cheap internationally. Having spent the past five years living in […]

The post Letter to the editor: Is South African wine really too cheap? appeared first on winemag.
content:
The following received via email from Louis Vigneault-Dubois, a former diplomat and WSET Level 2-certified wine enthusiast:

Last week, I read Tim Atkin’s annual South Africa Special Report with great interest, and one argument in particular stayed with me: that South African wines remain too cheap internationally.

Having spent the past five years living in South Africa and discovering its extraordinary wine scene, I have a lot of sympathy for that view. But after recently moving back to Germany, I’m seeing the question of value from a different perspective.

Let’s look at white wine in particular. A small moment in a wine shop recently summed it up perfectly.

On a hot August evening, a young woman walked in looking for a fresh white wine to take to an open-air concert with friends. Her budget was around €15 (R280).

The cheapest South African white on the shelf was Ken Forrester Old Vine Reserve Chenin Blanc at €18 (R335). The next on the price scale was Luddite Saboteur White at €24 (R450).

A few shelves away were several excellent German Rieslings, Pinot Gris and more at €15–16 (R280–300), some even carrying the VDP Erste Lage designation, loosely comparable to Premier Cru.

The salesperson made a convincing case for the Ken Forrester Chenin. But the customer chose a German white.

Not because it was necessarily better. It was slightly cheaper, more familiar and felt like the safer choice.

That small interaction captures what I think is one of the challenges facing South African wine in Europe.

The producer’s price isn’t the consumer’s value

I completely agree that many South African growers are not paid enough. Old vines, low yields and quality viticulture are expensive and increasingly difficult to sustain at current prices.

But what producers need to charge and what international consumers perceive as value are two different questions.

Many of the interesting South African wines I encounter in Germany seem to start around €20 and quickly move into the €30–40 range and above. For an enthusiast who understands what an old-vine Chenin from the Swartland or Stellenbosch represents, these wines can offer exceptional value.

For the broader consumer, however, €30 or €40 is already firmly premium territory.

Competition is fierce

In Germany, the €10–20 segment for white wine is packed with excellent Riesling, Grauburgunder and Weissburgunder, alongside Austrian Grüner Veltliner, Italian and Spanish whites, Loire Sauvignon Blanc, Rhône blends and entry-level Chablis.

Consumers are not only faced with an enormous range of familiar alternatives; many European producers also prominently market their organic, biodynamic or sustainability credentials, messages that may resonate more strongly with today’s European consumer than, for example, an old-vine certification.

What I see far less often are compelling South African whites in that price category that can persuade a curious but relatively casual wine drinker to take a chance on the Cape.

South Africa certainly has the story: extraordinary old vines, distinctive terroirs and a generation of exceptional winemakers. Critics know it. Serious wine lovers increasingly know it.

But the average European consumer probably doesn’t know what Stellenbosch, Swartland or Hemel-en-Aarde represent, let alone who Eben Sadie, Chris Alheit or the Mullineux are.

And as prices rise, that lack of recognition matters even more. A €20 South African Chenin is no longer competing simply with other Chenins. It is competing for the same money a consumer might spend on a serious German Riesling, a Chablis, Sancerre or any number of established European wines and regions backed by decades, sometimes centuries, of consumer recognition.

For South African producers and grape growers, the uncomfortable reality is that making excellent wine and having a compelling story is not enough. Plenty of other wine regions can offer both.

Among casual drinkers, price remains a crucial part of the value equation. And this is where South Africa seems to struggle: consumers can often find very good wines from more familiar regions at a cheaper price. However good the South African bottle may be, that makes it a harder choice on the shelf.

Bridging the price gap

The answer for the industry, therefore, cannot simply be to push prices upwards. It also has to be about strengthening the value proposition and building recognition across different price points.

Someone who discovers a brilliant South African Chenin for €10 today is far more likely to spend €30, €50 or €60 on a serious bottle tomorrow. But if the choice is between an €6 supermarket “dry white” and a €30 specialist bottle, we are asking consumers to skip several rungs of the ladder.

South Africa needs those intermediate rungs: wines that are accessible enough to encourage discovery, distinctive enough to create an association with the Cape, widely available enough to build recognition, and compelling enough to make consumers want to take the next step.

Ultimately, the question may not be whether South African wine is really too cheap internationally, but whether it has the right proposition at every level of the market to bring consumers along on the journey, from an accessible first bottle, to the middle ground, and eventually to the country’s great wines.

The quality is already there at the top. The challenge is building the steps that lead consumers there.

content:
Rules

  • Wines must be certified as South African and made from Certified Heritage Vineyards (vines that are 35 years and older vines registered with SAWIS and approved by the Old Vine Project).
  • Wines entered must be current release or soon to be released (minimum stock requirement: 50 x 6 bottles). Producers may enter as many different wines as they see fit.
  • An entry sample takes the form of two bottles. There are two submission methods – please indicate the number corresponding to your chosen option on the entry form:
  1. collection by Aspiring Couriers (login and create a waybill here)
  2. delivery to Aspiring Couriers
  • Entries close Wednesday 7 October. The deadline for the submission of samples is 17h00 on Thursday 8 October. LATE SUBMISSIONS WILL NOT BE ACCEPTED.
  • In the event a wine achieves Top 10 status, 18 bottles must be set aside at no charge, these to be served at promotional events.

To enter, kindly ensure you (or the company you represent) are a subscriber to Winemag.co.za. If you’re not yet subscribed, click here to sign up.

An entry fee of R1,495 including VAT per wine applies and you will be directed to our online shop to make payment after you have completed the entry form below. Please note that if you want to enter multiple wines, each will require a separate form although payment can be made all at once.

title: Aspiring Top Drop Awards 2026: 22 wines delivering exceptional value
summary:
We tasted 92 wines retailing for R120 or less. Twenty-two scored 91 points or higher, qualifying them to carry the Top Drop sticker. The post Aspiring Top Drop Awards 2026: 22 wines delivering exceptional value appeared first on winemag.
content:
We tasted 92 wines retailing for R120 or less. Twenty-two scored 91 points or higher, qualifying them to carry the Top Drop sticker.

From these, we’ve selected 10 standout buys – wines that combine particularly high quality with an especially attractive price. The remaining 12 also qualify as Top Drops and are listed below.

Top 10 Best Buys

Ranked by quality, with price considered in assessing overall value.

1. Nederburg Baronne 2024

44% Cabernet Sauvignon, 42% Shiraz, the rest Petit Verdot, Tannat, Durif, Malbec and Carignan. Engaging aromatics of red and black berries, fynbos, flowers and a hint of pepper. Light-bodied with fresh acidity and a gently savoury finish. Not massively intense in terms of weight or flavour, but by no means simple – unshowy and highly likeable.

Score:

93

Price:

R100

2. Wild House Chardonnay 2025 (Wildeberg)

Top notes of flowers and herbs before lemon, peach and the merest hint of vanilla on the nose while the palate is rich and textured but equally vital thanks to vibrant acidity. Well balanced and rather seductive.

Score:

93

Price:

R110

3. De Wet Chenin Blanc 2026

Very primary and inviting aromatics of guava, citrus and peach plus hints of flowers and herbs. The palate is clean and fresh with good fruit concentration, crisp acidity and a dry finish. Well balanced and entirely unassuming.

Score:

92

Price:

R69

4. Riebeek Cellars Collection Shiraz 2025

Just a little flinty reduction gives way to red berries, fynbos, rose and white pepper on the nose. The palate is light-bodied with juicy fruit, fresh acidity and fine tannins, with a faint savoury quality to the finish. Modest in scale but full of appeal.

Score:

92

Price: 

R88

5. Leyland Chenin Blanc 2026 (De Wet)

Aromatics of herbs, lime, lemon, a hint of guava and touch of leesy complexity. The palate has good weight and texture, with moderate acidity providing balance and a gently savoury finish bringing it to a neat close.

Score:

92

Price: 

R90

6. Durbanville Hills Cabernet Sauvignon 2024

Red and black berries, some leafiness, with a pleasant hint of smokiness on the nose. The palate is clean and fresh with fine tannins, the finish dry. True to the variety, unimposing, honest.

Score:

92

Price: 

R100

7. Koelenbosch Shiraz 2023 (Koelenhof)

The nose shows red and black berries, a touch of violets and black pepper. The palate is luscious and juicy with moderate acidity and a gently savoury finish.

Score:

92

Price: 

R105

8. Bellingham Homestead Sauvignon Blanc 2025

Herbal notes lead into bell pepper, grapefruit, granadilla and pineapple on the nose. The palate is rich and rounded, with well-integrated, tangy acidity and a gently savoury finish. At this price, it’s difficult to ask for much more.

Score:

92

Price: 

R115

9. Zorgvliet Silver Myn Argentum 2024

56% Merlot, 27% Cabernet Franc, 14% Cabernet Sauvignon, 3% Petit Verdot. Red and black berries, violets, a leafy note, earth and meat stock on the nose. Medium bodied with juicy fruit, good freshness and fine tannins. Lively with a nicely savoury finish. Classic in style, unshowy in execution.

Score:

92

Price: 

R118

10. Salt Rock Chenin Blanc 2025

Attractive aromatics of honeysuckle, herbs, citrus and green apple. The palate has concentrated fruit yet comes across as taut and austere in structure, with punchy acidity and a particularly dry finish. Elegant and nuanced.

Score:

92

Price: 

R120

Also Top Drop

These 12 wines also scored 91 points or higher and retail for R120 or less.

What is a Top Drop?

Top Drop is Winemag’s shortlist of wines that combine high quality with affordability. To qualify, a wine had to retail for R120 or less and score at least 91 points in our tasting.

Look for the Top Drop sticker in stores.

Winner benefits

Each category winner received R5,000 in shipping from Aspiring Couriers.

title: Burgundy dominates the world’s most expensive wines
summary:
Burgundy’s dominance at the top end of the fine-wine market is extraordinary. Investment platform WineCap’s 2026 ranking of the 25 most expensive wines contains 24 Burgundies, with only Domaine Jean-Louis Chave’s Ermitage Cathelin from the northern Rhône breaking the region’s hold. Even more striking, 17 wines come from Domaine Leroy and Domaine d’Auvenay, both owned […]

The post Burgundy dominates the world’s most expensive wines appeared first on winemag.
content:
Burgundy’s dominance at the top end of the fine-wine market is extraordinary. Investment platform WineCap’s 2026 ranking of the 25 most expensive wines contains 24 Burgundies, with only Domaine Jean-Louis Chave’s Ermitage Cathelin from the northern Rhône breaking the region’s hold.

Even more striking, 17 wines come from Domaine Leroy and Domaine d’Auvenay, both owned by Lalou Bize-Leroy, together accounting for 64.1% of the ranking’s combined value.

At the top is Domaine de la Romanée-Conti’s Romanée-Conti Grand Cru at £195,406 per 12-bottle case (roughly equivalent to R352,000 a bottle at today’s exchange rate), followed by Domaine d’Auvenay’s Chevalier-Montrachet Grand Cru at £186,419 per case (R336,000 a bottle).

For perspective, Pétrus, Bordeaux’s highest-ranked wine, sits only 46th in the wider ranking, while Krug Clos du Mesnil, Champagne’s highest entry, is 80th.

The lesson is fairly simple. At the very top of the wine market, scarcity, provenance and reputation can count for more than points. Burgundy happens to possess extraordinary quantities of all three – but the remarkable concentration of value around Lalou Bize-Leroy suggests that, at this level, the market is pricing not just wine but access to something that cannot readily be reproduced.

title: Jamie Goode: Old vines won’t survive on sentiment alone
summary:
Wine has been going through some changes. It has always been going through changes, to be honest. In classic wine-producing regions, we’ve had a long shift from the need for large quantities of cheap wine to feed the heroic thirst of the masses. People in Portugal, France, Italy and Spain used to drink a lot […]

The post Jamie Goode: Old vines won’t survive on sentiment alone appeared first on winemag.
content:
Wine has been going through some changes. It has always been going through changes, to be honest. In classic wine-producing regions, we’ve had a long shift from the need for large quantities of cheap wine to feed the heroic thirst of the masses. People in Portugal, France, Italy and Spain used to drink a lot of wine. The big need was for volume, and so industries geared to supply lots of cheap wine have been retrofitted to produce better quality wine for a more discerning and less thirsty customer base. It has been an uncomfortable process, and it’s still ongoing. In other countries wine has been growing and people have been drinking more, but even this growth has seen a bit of contraction of late. And it’s uncomfortable to watch, because people and their livelihoods are impacted.

The danger is that in this contraction process, it’s not only the less impressive vineyards that are being pulled out, but also some rather special vineyards. A case in point is in the notorious vine pull in Australia in the 1980s, where some very special old vineyards in regions such as the Barossa were taken out. Because of the absence of phylloxera in South Australia, the Barossa has a lot of old, ungrafted vines. There are more than 100 hectares of centenarian vineyards there.

And in Spain, were it not for the efforts of Comando G and their buddies, many of the amazing old Garnacha vineyards that simply weren’t profitable would have been pulled out. It’s strange how fashion changes: in the peak Parker era everyone wanted big, dark, bold wines – something that Garnacha can’t do easily. Now we cherish the fragrant, lighter-coloured reds that old vine Garnacha is an absolute specialist at.

Globally, there are many special old vineyards. They are a treasure, but they aren’t always treasured. Should there be laws protecting them?

When I was at university, one of the courses I took in my degree in biological science was on conservation and wildlife management. I really enjoyed it, to the point that I even considered doing a research job in ecology. There were two things I took away from this course. One is that if you want to conserve rare species, you need to focus on preserving their habitat. The second was that the only conservation that really works is conservation that pays. If an ecosystem or a species becomes an economic resource, then people will preserve them.

This is exactly the approach that has been taken by the Old Vine Project in South Africa, and it has been fantastic to watch this amazing initiative develop. And I guess imitation is the sincerest form of flattery: the model has been adopted by others. When Rosa Kruger set out to produce a list of vineyards over 35 years old in South Africa, this gave producers in search of old vines a chance to connect with growers. Previously, the fruit from many of these vineyards was being sold too cheaply, and disappearing into big blends where its origin was never recognized.

How do you keep precious old vineyards in the ground, rather than let them be bulldozed? I guess you could give them protected status, but for a vineyard to continue, it has to be farmed, and you can’t force a farmer to maintain a vineyard if they aren’t making money for it. And governments can’t easily pay farmers to preserve some vineyards and not others.

The best way to keep great vines in the ground is to value them. And the Old Vine Project does just this. Winemakers with ambition buy grapes from heritage vineyards and pay a premium that makes farming them pay. The growers are rewarded, and the bulldozers stay away. The Old Vine heritage seal is a great initiative here, and it means that suddenly cooperatives who were previously putting old vine grapes into an inexpensive wine can now make a separate wine from the old vines, add the heritage sticker, and charge R200 for the bottle. The seal acts as a strong buying cue. Everyone benefits.

Part of the dynamic here is having ambitious landless winemakers who want to make something special, and are able to because there is a culture of growers owning vineyards who are willing to sell these grapes. South Africa has a nice dynamic where winemakers working for large companies are allowed to do a bit of home brew: to start their own brand. Sometimes there are restrictions: perhaps a case limit of the new brand, or a stipulation that they use varieties other than used by their employer, to avoid conflict of interest situations. But the general permissiveness of winery owners in allowing their winemakers to have side projects is good for everyone, I think. It keeps the winemaker fulfilled professionally, it allows them to build their own brand gradually, and the dynamism created by new producers and new projects is good for the overall health of South African wine.

And, of course, this creates customers for old heritage vineyards, keeping them in the ground.

On a regional level, there is something to be said for legislation to protect significant vineyards. This is important where land has value for redevelopment. If it is zoned so that no one can build homes, but it has to be kept as agricultural land, then this is valuable. Urban spread is threatening many wine regions, and some legislation could help here. I was recently in the Hunter Valley, a brilliant historically significant Australian wine region. With its proximity to Sydney, this is quite a playground for city folk. If economics is left to decide the destiny of the land, then it’s likely that the vineyard area will further contract. You could end up with a wine region popular with tourists, but with hardly any vineyards.

But the best way to preserve important vineyards? Make them pay!

  • Jamie Goode is a London-based wine writer, lecturer, wine judge and book author. With a PhD in plant biology, he worked as a science editor, before starting wineanorak.com, one of the world’s most popular wine websites.
